approved: National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Small Amount Credit Contract and Consumer Lease Reforms) Bill 2018
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that would tighten rules on payday loans and rent-to-buy schemes.
The bill would cap total payments on consumer leases, require equal repayments on small loans, and ban door-to-door selling of leases at homes.
It would also let regulations reduce the protected earnings limit for Centrelink recipients from 20 per cent of gross income to 10 per cent of net income.
Caps total payments under a consumer lease.
Forces small amount credit contracts to have equal repayments and equal payment intervals.
Stops SACC providers from charging monthly fees on the remaining loan term when a customer repays early.
Bans lessors and credit assistance providers from selling leases door-to-door at homes.
Adds broad anti-avoidance protections for SACC and consumer lease providers.
Raises penalties to encourage compliance by SACC providers and lessors.
Borrowers using small amount credit contracts and consumer leases, and the providers of those products.

The motion noted the government's $200 billion defence investment as an opportunity for Australian businesses, congratulated the government on initiatives including the 2016 Defence White Paper and the Centre for Defence Industry Capability, and encouraged small and medium enterprises to seek defence contracts.

The speech supported the National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Small Amount Credit Contract and Consumer Lease Reforms) Bill, citing cases of exploitation such as a $150 loan ballooning to over $1,000 and a Centrelink recipient left with $50 after deductions, and urged passage of the bill to ban door-to-door sales and introduce anti-avoidance protections.

The speaker criticised the government for repeatedly delaying promised legislation to regulate small-amount credit contracts and consumer leases, arguing the reforms are needed to protect vulnerable Australians from exploitative lenders. They noted the bill would cap total payments under consumer leases, ban monthly fees on early loan repayments, and strengthen penalties, and urged the government to pass it without further delay.

The speaker argued that payday lenders exploit vulnerable low-income Australians, causing spiralling debt and financial stress, particularly in the Lalor electorate where postcode 3030 is the ninth-highest hotspot for small-amount credit contracts. He supported the National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Small Amount Credit Contract and Consumer Lease Reforms) Bill 2018, which would cap loan repayments at 10% of net income, and criticised the member for Deakin for failing to bring the bill to parliament earlier.
